intro.heading: The evidence exists. It is just not in one place.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: The email arrives on a Tuesday. A visitor from the local authority commissioning team will come on the following Thursday for a quality assurance visit. The manager is calm, because the home is run well. Then she starts to list what she might want to show: last month's audits, the medication action that was fixed, the policy review dates, who attended the fire session. They all exist. They sit in a binder, a shared drive, an email thread and a few heads. Nobody has pulled them together, and nobody has checked them against each other.

trail.text: The email arrives. A visit is booked for next Thursday.
The manager knows the home is run well and the audits are done.
She writes a list of what she could show, starting with the audit reports.
The audit PDFs are in one place. The action photos are in another.
Nobody is sure which policies are still current or have gone stale.
Training sign in sheets are in a folder. Who understood the session is not.
The list is long, the folder is thin, and time is short.
“Can you show me how you know this is working?”

trail_close: The care was never the problem. The gap is between what you do and what you can show quickly. Here is how CareStream helps you gather it, and where you still have to do the last step yourself.

why.heading: A visitor asks how you know, not just what you do
why.sub: Good care and good evidence are two jobs. The second one is the one that gets left until the week before.

cards.title: Evidence is scattered by habit
cards.body: Audit reports, photos, policy files and sign in sheets are created at different times by different people. Nobody planned to find them all in one afternoon.

cards.title: Old policies are easy to miss
cards.body: A policy that still names a body that has since been replaced, or still has an unfilled placeholder, can sit unnoticed until someone outside reads it.

cards.title: Paper shows attendance, not understanding
cards.body: A signed sheet shows who was in the room. A visitor may also talk to staff, so what they remember matters as much as what the folder says.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most before a visit.

items.q: Is there one button that gives me everything for the visit?
items.a: No, and we would rather say so now. Your evidence sits in a few places: audit reports, closed actions, the policy checks, the policy usage report and the face to face records. What CareStream does is keep them all in one system, so you gather and print them in an afternoon.

items.q: Does CareStream tell me what the commissioner will ask for?
items.a: No. A commissioner visit is not a CQC inspection, and what a visitor wants to see is up to them. Ask your commissioning contact what they would like in advance, then use CareStream to find it quickly.

items.q: What can I pull from my audits?
items.a: Each completed audit has a PDF report with its scores, photos and actions. Action owners can add up to 10 photos as proof, and the next audit of the same kind marks earlier actions as fixed or not fixed. Audits are free on every plan, though the drafted recommendations need a paid plan.

items.q: Can it check my policies before the visit?
items.a: Yes, in two ways. The out of date scan flags old terms, placeholder text and overdue reviews with no tokens used. Gap detection looks for what is missing from your policy set and is on Professional and above, while the Free plan screens up to 5 uploaded policies. Suggestions stay suggestions until an admin adopts them.

items.q: Will CareStream predict my CQC rating?
items.a: No. The CQC readiness score is our own blend of your audit results and your policy coverage. It is a guide for you, not a CQC rating, and it cannot say how any visit will go.

items.q: What about staff who get questioned?
items.a: CQC Staff Prep gives staff practice questions by job role, so they can rehearse answering in their own words. It is practice and not a simulation of any visit. You can also allocate short training from your own policies, and a wrong answer becomes a short lesson in the Staff Hub.

items.q: What does the policy usage report show?
items.a: The CQC Inspection Evidence Report shows how staff have used your policies over a period you choose, 12 months by default. It is on Professional and above. You print it or save it as a PDF from your browser. It shows use, not a pass or a rating.

items.q: Can I try it before the visit, and what does it cost?
items.a: Yes. There is a 14 day free trial on the paid plans, and you can create a free account to run audits and screen up to 5 policies. See the pricing page for plans, or create a free account to start.

items.q: What is a quality assurance visit in a care setting?
items.a: It is a visit from outside the service to look at how it is run, often from a local authority or commissioning team. What they look at depends on them, so ask them before the day. It is not the same as a CQC inspection.

items.q: What happens at a commissioner visit?
items.a: That varies, and we cannot say what any commissioner will require. Ask your contact what they will want to see and who they want to speak to. Then use your audits, policies and staff records to answer quickly.

items.q: How far ahead should I start gathering evidence?
items.a: As soon as the date is confirmed. A few days lets you find gaps, such as an overdue review or an action that was never re-checked, and fix them before the visit.

items.q: Is a commissioner visit the same as a CQC inspection?
items.a: No. They are different visits with different purposes. Evidence that supports one often helps with the other, which is why keeping it in one place is useful.

items.q: What if I find a gap while I gather my evidence?
items.a: Fix it, record that you fixed it and keep the trail. An action closed with a photo and re-checked at the next audit tells a better story than a folder that hides the problem.

items.q: What counts as CQC evidence for a care home?
items.a: It is the record that shows how you assess and improve your service, such as audits, actions, policies and staff records. Our guide to CQC evidence categories sets out how it is usually grouped.

items.q: Is there a CQC inspection checklist I can use?
items.a: A checklist helps you find gaps, but it does not replace the record behind it. Our inspection day guide covers what to prepare, and your audits supply the evidence for each point.

items.q: Does the law say I need to monitor quality?
items.a: Regulation 17 says systems or processes must be established and operated effectively, and that they must let the registered person assess, monitor and improve the quality and safety of the services provided. Read the wording of Regulation 17. Audits are one way to do this.

items.q: Does CareStream show how I assess risk?
items.a: Audit reports show what you checked and what you did about it. Regulation 12 requires you to assess the risks to service users and do all that is reasonably practicable to mitigate them, and audit actions are one record of this.

guide.heading: A practical way to prepare for a quality assurance visit
guide.lede: Preparing for a visit is easier when you treat it as a short project. Pick a day, gather in a set order and check each item before you close the folder.

sections.h3: Start by asking the visitor what they want to see
paragraphs: A commissioner visit can look at many things, and no list from us will match theirs. A short email asking what they would like to see, and whether they plan to speak to staff or residents, saves a lot of guessing. Under Regulation 17, services need systems to assess, monitor and improve quality, so most visitors will expect some record of how you do that.

sections.h3: A CQC inspection checklist for your evidence folder
checklist: Audit reports: the last three months of PDFs, with action outcomes and re-check results.
Closed actions: the photos and notes that show each problem was fixed.
Policies: run the out of date scan and fix flagged terms, placeholders and overdue reviews.
Staff records: the policy usage report and the sign in sheets for recent sessions, on Professional and above.

sections.h3: Check what staff remember, not just what is filed
paragraphs: If the visitor may speak to staff, give them a short practice round. CQC Staff Prep sets practice questions by job role, and a short training module on the home's own policies shows who needs another look. Keep these results with your CQC evidence, and note anything you improved before the day.

guide.note: On the day. Bring the folder, but also know where each item lives in the system. If the visitor asks for something you did not print, you can find it in minutes.
